Two years ago, my team used to do everything by hand. When a developer needed a new test environment, they used to open a ticket and wait. I was the person who approved every request, so I was the bottleneck. The turnaround time used to be about a week, and people found a workaround: they shared old environments, and that created new problems. Then we decided to automate the whole process. Today, a developer clicks one button and gets an environment in twenty minutes. I don't approve anything anymore; the rules do. The biggest lesson learned for me was simple. If one person is in the middle of every request, that person is the problem, even with good intentions.

I didn't use to like retrospectives. In my old company, we used to have a two-hour meeting at the end of every project, and nobody wanted to talk about mistakes. We used to write a long document, and nobody read it. Now I run them differently. We meet after the first month, not at the end, because there is still time to change things. The meeting takes thirty minutes, and we answer only three questions: what used to slow us down, what is better now, and what we want to streamline next month. Every answer needs a name and a date. It sounds simple, but it changed the culture of my team. People don't hide problems anymore, because a problem is just the next thing to fix.
